title: Sony Bank, Fujitsu apply generative AI at full scale for financial system
excerpt: Frontier Tech. AI & ML. News. Share. Facebook. X. WhatsApp. Linkedin. Sony Bank and Fujitsu are applying generative AI at full scale in the development of Sony Bank’s core banking system. By establishing a mechanism for AI to utilize development assets such as design documents, source code, and test assets, and gradually expanding its application to key processes from design to manufacturing and testing through actual development, the companies have confirmed a 30% reduction in the development period from basic design to integration testing as of July 2026, compared to conventional methods. The system adopts Fujitsu’s core banking solution, Fujitsu Core Banking xBank, which features a cloud-native architecture operating on Amazon Web Services (AWS), providing an environment that enables rapid integration and trials with generative AI services. This environment allowed for the phased application of generative AI to each process. In this initiative, an AI agent centered on Anthropic PBC’s Claude on Amazon Bedrock is utilized across processes, with human oversight for final judgment and quality assurance. The use of generative AI is not limited to proof-of-concept (PoC) but has been established as a development process for a core banking system in live operation. Sony Bank and Fujitsu will leverage the knowledge and development assets gained from this initiative to other processes and systems, further deepening and expanding the use of generative AI at Sony Bank. Fujitsu will also apply the knowledge gained from this initiative to future Core Banking xBank development and development for other financial institutions, contributing to the advancement of financial system development. In this initiative, generative AI transforms the entire development process by leveraging design documents, source code, and test assets across all stages. This initiative has resulted in a 40% reduction in man-hours and a 30% reduction in development period for processes from basic design to integration testing. Specifically, the companies confirmed up to a 90% reduction in impact assessment man-hours in the basic design phase, up to a 40% reduction in design document creation man-hours in the detailed design phase, a 99% source code generation rate in the implementation phase, and up to a 90% reduction in test execution man-hours in the integration testing phase. Sony Bank and Fujitsu intend to proceed with the application of generative AI to the entire development process, including requirements definition, and gradually expand its application to security, operations, and maintenance areas. Further, the knowledge and development assets gained from this initiative will be utilized in peripheral systems, further deepening and expanding the use of generative AI at Sony Bank. Sony Bank aims to become an “AI-native bank” that can quickly respond to changing customer needs and business environments by continuously utilizing AI. Also, Fujitsu plans to extend this model to other financial institutions adopting Core Banking xBank, supporting the broader modernization of banking systems in Japan. The knowledge and feedback gained from this initiative will also be utilized in the development of the Uvance for Finance AI Transformation Platform, a dedicated AI platform that supports AI utilization for financial institutions, aiming for further sophistication of AI-driven system development. Additionally, through Uvance for Finance, which enhances financial operations with data and AI, Fujitsu will accelerate system development for financial institutions and advance the continuous transformation of financial services. Tatsuya Fukushima, executive officer at Sony Bank, said that the successful full-scale application of generative AI to the development of our production core banking system is a significant step towards becoming a bank that continuously evolves based on AI. “We will continue to promote our evolution into an AI-native bank while ensuring safety and q

title: Visa warnt vor neuen Cyberrisiken durch KI
summary: Der Kreditkarten- und Zahlungsdienstleister Visa warnt vor einer neuen Generation von Cyberangriffen, die mit Hilfe künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) eigenständig lernen und sich an Abwehrmassnahmen anpassen könnten. Das Unternehmen hat nach eigenen Angaben Teile seines KI-gestützten Systems zur Cyberabwehr als Open-Source-Software veröffentlicht.
excerpt: Leben & Karriere. Fintech. Mediathek. English News. Middle East. Asia. Advertorials. Newsletter. Über uns. Werbung. Suche. Mittwoch, 30. September 2026. Visa warnt vor neuen Cyberrisiken durch KI. Der Kreditkarten- und Zahlungsdienstleister Visa warnt vor einer neuen Generation von Cyberangriffen, die mit Hilfe künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) eigenständig lernen und sich an Abwehrmassnahmen anpassen könnten. Das Unternehmen hat nach eigenen Angaben Teile seines KI-gestützten Systems zur Cyberabwehr als Open-Source-Software veröffentlicht. (Bild: Shutterstock). Mittwoch, 30. September 2026 12:12. Von York Runne | Redaktor. Visa warnt vor neuen Cyberrisiken durch KI. Visa-Technologiechef Rajat Taneja sagte gegenüber der Nachrichtenagentur «Reuters» , Schwachstellen, die Anfang des Jahres durch das KI-Modell Mythos des US-Startups Anthropic sichtbar geworden seien, hätten der Branche die Dimension der Herausforderungen klar gemacht. Die Erkenntnisse seien «demütigend» gewesen. Taneja verwies zudem auf einen Angriff von KI-Agenten auf die Softwareplattform Hugging Face. Der Vorfall könne ein erster Vorgeschmack auf künftig deutlich weitreichendere Angriffe sein. «Es ist schwer vorherzusagen, wie schlimm es werden könnte, aber wir haben den Trailer gesehen», sagte Taneja. KI-Modelle hätten dabei unter anderem die Grenzen einer Testumgebung überwunden. Künftig könnten Cyberangriffe laut Taneja zunehmend autonom, anpassungsfähig und lernfähig sein. Angreifer könnten dadurch einen erheblichen Vorteil erhalten. «Wenn der Angreifer agentenbasiert ist, muss auch die Verteidigung agentenbasiert sein. Andernfalls besteht ein Ungleichgewicht», so der IT-Manager weiter. KI-Agenten werden selbst zu Kunden. Die Entwicklung ist für Visa auch deshalb relevant, weil das Unternehmen bereits bestimmten KI-Agenten ermöglicht, Zahlungen über sein Netzwerk abzuwickeln. Taneja machte keine Angaben dazu, wie viele Transaktionen bereits auf diese Weise erfolgen. Branchenprognosen zufolge könnten KI-Agenten bis 2030 für rund ein Drittel des Onlinehandels verantwortlich sein. Das entspräche einem Transaktionsvolumen von rund 3,1 Billionen Dollar. Damit steigt zugleich die Bedeutung von Sicherheitsmechanismen, die nicht nur menschliche Nutzer, sondern auch autonom handelnde Software schützen und kontrollieren können. Quantencomputer als langfristiges Risiko. Neben KI sieht Visa langfristig auch im Quantencomputing eine Bedrohung für die Sicherheit des globalen Zahlungsverkehrs. Taneja verwies auf Shors Algorithmus, mit dem leistungsfähige Quantencomputer eines Tages heute gängige Verschlüsselungsverfahren brechen könnten. Unternehmen müssten deshalb weiter daran arbeiten, die Risiken für die Verschlüsselung zu begrenzen, sagte er. «Wir müssen optimistisch sein. Aber es gibt keine einfache Antwort. ». Visa veröffentlicht damit einen Teil seiner Abwehrtechnologie als Open Source, während Unternehmen und Regulierungsbehörden weltweit nach Wegen suchen, die wachsenden Risiken durch autonome KI-Systeme und künftige Quantencomputer für die Finanzinfrastruktur einzudämmen. Das Unternehmen wickelt nach eigenen Angaben rund eine Milliarde Zahlungen pro Tag mit einem jährlichen Volumen von etwa 15 Billionen Dollar ab. Damit gehört das Unternehmen zu den zentralen Akteuren der globalen Zahlungsinfrastruktur und ist zugleich in besonderem Masse auf das Vertrauen in die Sicherheit seiner Systeme angewiesen. title: The rise of agentic payments: When treasury systems become autonomous bankers
excerpt: . AI-powered treasury agents are reshaping payments, challenging banks to build a new digital trust architecture. The treasurer has left the chat. Corporate treasury is entering a new phase of digital evolution. While automation, APIs, and straight-through processing have become standard, the next wave of innovation is being driven by agentic AI embedded directly within treasury management systems (TMS). Leading providers are beginning to introduce agentic AI-powered capabilities that go beyond reporting and insights. These capabilities enable treasury platforms to analyze liquidity, recommend actions, and orchestrate workflows with minimal human intervention. As agentic AI-driven treasury platforms become the primary decision layer for organizations, banks face an uncomfortable reality: user experience alone will no longer differentiate them. When agents rather than humans choose rails, products, and liquidity options, traditional banking payments expertise might lose some of its value to AI agents. This expertise includes knowledge about rail characteristics, cutoffs, corridor pricing, correspondent chains, format quirks, value-date arithmetic, and operations. Rather than relying solely on traditional channels such as ERP integrations, host-to-host connectivity, APIs, or batch file transfers, banks will need to support a new class of interactions. These interactions will be initiated by treasury agents acting on behalf of corporate users. Such AI agents may request liquidity information, evaluate funding options, initiate treasury actions, or trigger payment workflows based on predefined policies and governance controls. This shift creates a fundamental challenge for transaction banks: how to securely enable machine-to-machine financial interactions while preserving trust, accountability, and regulatory compliance. Know your agent: The new digital trust architecture. Know your agent (KYA) applies know your customer (KYC) principles to AI agents, requiring banks to verify an agent’s identity, authority, and actions just as they would for a human customer. The key challenge goes beyond granting access. Banks need clear, auditable proof that the agent was authorized to act on behalf of a client for a specific purpose and session. Retail payments have already begun addressing this reality through agentic protocols. Examples include Google’s AP2, Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol, and Mastercard’s Agent Pay. These protocols all assume a natural-person principal, a card rail, a merchant counterparty, and a network rulebook with an adjudication mechanism behind it. Corporate treasury has none of these four elements. Corporate banking is still in the early stages of understanding what machine-initiated financial activity means. Despite significantly larger transaction values and more complex approval structures, it lacks an equivalent banking framework or protocol. Corporate banking faces a significant challenge because many authorization and control processes were designed for human users. It often depends on offline authorization, signature verification, and approvals in addition to credentials and access controls. As a result, banks need to establish how AI agents can obtain and demonstrate the same level of trusted, auditable authority to act on behalf of corporate clients. Banks must now answer a new question: How do we verify who the customer is, which AI agent is acting on their behalf, and the authority under which that agent is acting?. Engineering the trust layer for agentic banking. We see this as the next frontier of trust in financial services. Just as KYC became a foundational banking capability, KYA will become critical for enabling safe, scalable agentic banking. The real requirement goes beyond agent identification. Banks and corporations need machine-readable mandates that clearly define an agent’s authority. These mandates need to specify what an agent can do and which accounts and payment corridors it can access. The

title: What the First Papal Encyclical on AI Asks of Banks
excerpt: Technology. What the First Papal Encyclical on AI Asks of Banks. by internationalbanker September 30, 2026. September 30, 2026. 1 By Dr. Robert Straw , CEO, CEIBS Switzerland. T he Vatican has produced the most sustained account yet of what responsible artificial intelligence (AI) deployment looks like from outside the technology industry, and Brussels, Denver, Delaware and Beijing have already written its central demand into law. All five locate the safeguard in the same place: a human being who can understand, contest and stop the machine. None of them asks whether the deployment has left that person able to do so. For banks, whose entire model-risk doctrine rests on competent human challenge, that is the question of the decade. On May 15, 2026, Pope Leo XIV signed Magnifica Humanitas , the first papal encyclical on artificial intelligence. It runs to 245 numbered paragraphs under the subtitle “On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence”. The date was chosen rather than found. It was the 135th anniversary of Rerum Novarum , in which Pope Leo XIII confronted the factory system, mass industrialization and the reduction of workers to interchangeable labor; it helped set the terms on which industrial economies came to govern the treatment of working people. The signal is unsubtle. The Catholic Church intends to do for the age of artificial intelligence what it did for the age of the machine. Readers of this publication may reasonably ask what a teaching letter of the Catholic Church is doing in a discussion of bank governance. Nobody is suggesting that institutions adopt theology. The claim is narrower and harder to dismiss. First, outside standards of this kind migrate. Anyone who has lived through the climate and cybersecurity cycles will recognize the sequence: soft norms first, investor and stewardship questions second, disclosure rules and litigation third, with the substance largely written in the first phase by institutions that no bank controlled. Reading such a standard earlyis not piety. It is risk management. Second, and more practically, the letter singles out finance. It identifies financial automation and speculative instruments as a domain in which systemic risk is amplified and value becomes detached from the real economy. Much of the public AI debate concerns model capabilities, compute thresholds and international machinery. This document is almost entirely about deployment: what an institution does when it buys a system, points it at a population and switches it on. That is not the legislature’s or the laboratory’s layer; it is the bank’s. An unlikely convergence. The letter’s core demand is that for any consequential decision, a person must be able to account for it: to justify it, monitor it, contest it and put it right. The letter’s core demand is that for any consequential decision, a person must be able to account for it: to justify it, monitor it, contest it and put it right. Its reasoning is that these systems do not understand what they produce, hold no conscience and bear no consequences, so accountability cannot be delegated to something that cannot be held to answer. If no human can be named as answerable, the system is not ready to run. What makes this more than an ethical preference is that four other authorities have arrived at the same place from entirely different premises. The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) classifies creditworthiness assessment and risk pricing in life and health insurance as high-risk and requires such systems to be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them in use. Colorado became the first US state to impose a duty of reasonable care on deployers of high-risk systems, though it has since narrowed that law to a disclosure regime taking effect in January 2027, a reminder that the rules are still moving even where the principle is settled. excerpt: The European Union’s (EU) main financial regulator has made AI and tokenization—where assets are traded on blockchains rather than through traditional financial markets—key priorities for banking regulators in EU member states to focus on for 2027. The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) said it will work with national authorities to see how banks and other financial services firms use AI and tokenization to innovate while ensuring consumers and investors remain protected, adding that it “will remain flexible to address future technological developments as they emerge,” such as advanced “frontier” AI.
